5. Retiring physics risks for ARC Returning to Eddington, he concluded (Eddington 1920) with reference to the parable of Daedalus and Icarus:

Cautious Daedalus will apply his theories where he feels most confident they will safely go; but by his excess of caution their hidden weaknesses can not be brought to light. Icarus will strain his theories to the breaking-point till the weak joints gape. For a spectacular stunt? Perhaps partly; he is often very human. But if he is not yet destined to reach the sun and solve for all time the riddle of its constitution, yet he may hope to learn from his journey some hints to build a better machine.

Building new machines and major hardware enhancements – new experimental research platforms – have been the largest drivers of progress in fusion energy science. A key output from this set of papers analysing the ARC V3A design is to identify the remaining physics risks to inform the goals of early SPARC campaigns, where SPARC will be the critical risk retirement platform for ARC. ARC V3A does not represent a final design, but serves as a crucible for our current models and understanding of tokamak plasmas, to identify the specific questions research on SPARC will address, to allow us to build a better machine. The ARC tokamak design is not expected to be finalised until early SPARC results confirm or contradict key predictions; although, many aspects of the overall plant design and supporting systems can proceed based on design targets, without a detailed design of the vacuum vessel or of all tokamak systems. In several metrics, in particular for heat exhaust, SPARC will be more challenging than ARC, due to operation at higher poloidal magnetic field leading to a narrower scrape-off layer decay length, λq (Eich et al. 2026). SPARC is also predicted to be more susceptible to n = 1 error field mode locking than ARC; SPARC will retire important risks related to MHD stability for high-performance, high-magnetic-field tokamaks (Leuthold et al. 2026). SPARC is also predicted to have higher normalised electromagnetic loads from disruptions than ARC, and metrics for the runaway electron avalanche are similar between the two machines (Sweeney et al. 2026). This section discusses how SPARC can retire specific physics risks for ARC, as well as identifies physics risks outside the scope of SPARC operation associated with long-pulse operation. Along with this set of physics basis papers CFS is also making a set of digital assets, in machine-readable formats common in the field, describing ARC V3A publicly available, similar to the publicly available information on SPARC (SPARCPublic 2024). Appendix A provides a detailed description of the files, which we make available for input to codes and analysis by interested readers. (v) Disruptivity for an ARC-relevant scenario, with ARC-like control and diagnostics. (vi) Exploration of runaway electron generation and dynamics at high plasma current. (vii) Development of robust disruption-mitigation procedures to avoid surface melting. (viii) Extension of experimental confinement database to high magnetic field and validation of fusion performance predictions. (ix) Tearing mode stability and onset in low-rotation, high-performance plasmas in the presence of substantial alpha particles. (x) Alpha-driven instabilities and resulting fast particle redistribution and losses in alpha-heating-dominant plasmas. (xi) Validation of ripple loss predictions. (xii) RF impurity generation and demonstration of operation with minimal impurity accumulation. (xiii) Characterisation of hydrogen minority RF heating and near-antenna scrapeoff layer conditions in the ARC-relevant scenario. (xiv) Extension of experimental L–H transition threshold database to high magnetic field and density, to inform ARC auxiliary heating requirements and operation, and enable model development and testing. (xv) Operation at high scrape-off layer opaqueness to inform whether pellet fuelling is required in ARC. (xvi) Intrinsic rotation to inform neoclassical toroidal viscosity effects on error field correction, and rotation effects on MHD stability and impurity transport. (xvii) Impurity compression in the divertor, pedestal impurity screening and mitigation of tungsten accumulation. (xviii) Operation in high-performance double-null plasmas, with active control to maintain double-null configuration.

While the first mission for SPARC is demonstration of Q > 1, and SPARC is designed to achieve Q ∼10, the list above shows the broader context for early SPARC campaigns to retire physics risks for ARC, which will require scenario development to achieve and characterise an ARC-relevant scenario, and may require additional scenarios to achieve ARC-like normalised parameters relevant to different physics such as divertor power exhaust, alpha-driven instabilities or to match non-dimensional plasma parameters.

Risks associated with long-pulse operation can be mitigated via demonstration of high power, detached scenarios on experiments such as EAST, K-STAR, WEST and JT-60SA. Modelling and test facilities may mitigate risks associated with long time integrated effects such as material erosion and neutron damage, although synergetic material effects may only be evident via early ARC operation, and can then be taken into account in later replacement cycles of the ARC vacuum vessel.

6. Conclusions We have presented analysis of the plasma physics basis for the design and operation of ARC V3A, and highlighted specific risks to be retired through SPARC operation. The ARC design will continue to evolve through further physics and engineering design efforts, and in response to results from early SPARC operation. Together with the associated topical papers, this work comprises a rigorous assessment of the ARC V3A power plant design, and demonstrates a flexible and powerful set of workflows that will be deployed in further iterations of the ARC design, as engineering and physics analysis progresses, and in response to early results from SPARC campaigns. The workflows will continue to be developed as the ARC design matures to include detailed three-dimensional structure such as pumping ducts, refined dedicated neutron shielding and diagnostic ports, as well as actuator and control constraints, and will be improved following lessons learned from this exercise. A key output of this work is the granular identification of ARC physics risks, and assessment of model uncertainties for power-plant-relevant plasma conditions. This will be important for informing the priorities of early SPARC research. This path, via retiring physics risks for ARC through SPARC, represents the fastest approach to realising fusion power on the grid.

# Characterising fast ion losses in tokamaks with quasisymmetry metrics

Alexandra LeViness1 , Jon C. Hillesheim1 , Alexander J. Creely1 , Clayton E. Myers1 and Philip B. Snyder1

1Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Devens, USA Corresponding author: Alexandra LeViness, aleviness@cfs.energy

(Received 2 June 2026 UTC; revision received 28 August 2026 UTC; accepted 16 September 2026 UTC)

In this work, ARC and SPARC equilibria with randomly generated coil misalignments are analysed using the metric of quasisymmetry error, frequently used in stellarator theory as a proxy for fast ion conﬁnement, and a strong correlation between this metric and rippleinduced alpha power loss is found. In discussions of magnetic conﬁnement devices, it is often taken for granted that tokamaks, unlike stellarators, are devices with axisymmetric magnetic ﬁelds. However, any tokamak built from discrete toroidal ﬁeld (TF) coils will have non-axisymmetric components of the magnetic ﬁeld due to the effect of TF ripple, and these components only grow when inevitable assembly errors are taken into account. Physically constructed tokamaks therefore have magnetic ﬁelds which can best be classi- ﬁed as near axisymmetric, and which share many characteristics with quasi-axisymmetric stellarators, allowing both classes of devices to be analysed using similar methods.

Key words: fusion plasma, plasma conﬁnement

1. Introduction Tokamaks are commonly described as axisymmetric magnetic fusion devices, as opposed to stellarators, which have three-dimensional (3-D) magnetic fields. However, this is a simplification. While tokamaks approximate axisymmetry, every physically constructed tokamak will have variations in magnetic field strength with toroidal angle – primarily due to the use of discrete toroidal field (TF) coils, which create TF ripple, but also due to manufacturing and assembly errors, current leads and the presence of components such as ferritic inserts or runaway electron mitigation coils. In addition, it may be desirable to induce symmetry-breaking components in the field known as resonant magnetic perturbations (RMPs) for the mitigation of dangerous instabilities such as edge-localised modes (ELMs). Considering this, tokamaks might be considered not as axisymmetric devices, but as near-axisymmetric devices, with similarities to quasi-axisymmetric stellarators, and the class of near-quasisymmetric (QS) devices ought to be understood to include both tokamaks and a subset of stellarators. Quasisymmetry is a concept from stellarator theory which describes 3-D magnetic fields in which, in straight field line Boozer coordinates (Boozer 1981), the magnetic field strength B on any flux surface is

independent of a linear combination of the poloidal and toroidal angles (Helander 2014). It is a subtype of quasiomnigeneity, which describes 3-D magnetic fields in which trapped particle drift orbits have zero bounce-averaged radial component (Hall & McNamara 1975), which also requires that the second adiabatic invariant J|| be constant across all field lines on each flux surface (Landreman 2011). Quasi-axisymmetric (QA) fields are those in which B is independent of the toroidal Boozer angle φ, as in a perfectly 2-D field such as that of an ideal tokamak (Garabedian 1996). No device, however, is perfectly QA: it has been proven that perfect quasisymmetry can be achieved on no more than a single flux surface within a stellarator (Garren & Boozer 1991; Plunk & Helander 2018), and while idealised (axisymmetric) tokamaks are exempt from this limitation, in the real world, as previously discussed, a tokamak built with discrete coils can never have perfectly axisymmetric field strength. Considering this, all QA devices, both tokamaks and stellarators, are only near-QA approximations of true quasisymmetry. Stellarator equilibria with deviations from quasisymmetry smaller than the magnetic field of the Earth have been found (Landreman & Paul 2022), and it has become possible to find nearly perfectly quasiomnigeneous stellarator equilibria, whether QS or not (Dudt et al. 2024; Goodman et al. 2024), but like tokamaks, the necessity to generate these fields with real coils typically increases the deviations from quasisymmetry (Wechsung et al. 2022), and that is without yet considering the potential impact of errors in constructing and assembling these complex coils. Quasi-axisymmetric stellarators have neoclassical transport which is in many ways analogous to that of tokamaks, as in Boozer coordinates, the two device types are isomorphic (Boozer 1983). In particular, in both QA stellarators and tokamaks, trapped particles execute so-called banana orbits, and their plasmas tend to generate large bootstrap currents compared with non-QA stellarators. However, there are significant differences as well: stellarators (QA or otherwise) tend to see lower shear than tokamaks, particularly in the edge, which will impact transport in this region. Considering this, both tokamaks and QA stellarators should be considered as subclasses of the larger grouping of (near-)QA fields, and methods from ‘stellarator theory’ developed for this class of field, if not dependent on qualities specific to stellarators, may produce useful results when applied to tokamaks. For example, previous research has found that, by reducing deviations from quasiaxisymmetry, simulated losses of fast ions from stellarator equilibria can be reduced to negligible values, lower than even that of (idealised, 2-D) tokamaks (Landreman, Buller & Drevlak 2022). In addition, comparing several quantitative metrics of deviations from quasi-axisymmetry with simulated alpha power loss in power-plant-sized stellarators, correlation coefficients above 0.8 were found (LeViness et al. 2023). In this work, the latter method is applied to the SPARC and ARC tokamak designs with randomised coil misalignments, and a strong correlation between QA error and predicted alpha power loss is found, replicating previous results in near-QA stellarators. Section 2 will discuss simulations which were previously performed for ARC in Hillesheim et al. (2026) to determine the alpha power loss assuming different types and sizes of coil misalignments. Section 3 will explore the magnitude of deviations from quasi-axisymmetry in ARC, and the relationship between a quantitative measure of this error and predicted alpha power loss. Additional coil misalignment types outside of those explored in Hillesheim et al. (2026) will also be investigated. Section 4 will then apply the approach of analysing QA error to SPARC, considering possible coil misalignments which are within actual assembly tolerances

2. Fast ion loss simulations For this work, simulations for alpha transport and loss in the SPARC and ARC tokamaks were performed. SPARC is a tokamak currently under construction by Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) which aims to demonstrate net fusion energy (Q > 1), while ARC is the next-generation device, currently being designed, which is planned to be the first commercial fusion power plant and to deliver energy to the grid. Both are conventional aspect ratio tokamaks with coils made from hightemperature superconductor. SPARC has a major radius of 1.85 m and a minor radius of 0.57 m, with a magnetic field on axis of 12.2 T and plasma current of 8.7 MA at its design point, while ARC’s V3A design point has a major radius of 4.62 m, a minor radius of 1.18 m, a magnetic field on axis of 11.4 T and a plasma current of 12.0 MA. Further details of their designs can be found in the SPARC and ARC physics overview papers (Creely et al. 2020a; Hillesheim et al. 2026). In order to predict alpha power loss from these devices, simulations were performed with ASCOT5 (Varje 2022), a Monte Carlo orbit following code which has previously been validated against experimental data from devices like JET (Varje 2022), ASDEX Upgrade (Hynönen et al. 2007) and Wendelstein 7-X (Äkäslompolo et al. 2019), and has been used to predict alpha losses from ITER (Snicker, Sipilä & Kurki-Suonio 2012) as well as many other designed fusion devices. In the simulations performed for this work, alpha particles were generated randomly spaced throughout the outer flux surfaces of the plasma, weighted by the local fusion rate and followed in 3-D magnetic fields while being subjected to collisions determined by the predicted plasma density and temperature. No radial electric field or magnetohydrodynamic effects were included. Three-dimensional magnetic fields were calculated from realistic coil geometries represented by hundreds of individual filaments, taking into account possible coil-to-coil misalignments. These fields, which are the vacuum fields produced by the aligned or misaligned TF coil sets, were then combined with the axisymmetric poloidal field calculated by ASCOT5 from the poloidal flux of the base equilibrium, assuming that the non-axisymmetric component of the field is a small perturbation on top of the axisymmetric equilibrium. This method excludes not only the 3-D plasma response to the ripple, but also the plasma pressure contribution to the toroidal magnetic field, which, for the SPARC and ARC equilibria considered, increases the magnitude of the TF by up to 0.60 and 0.15 T at the core, respectively. The change to the field is minimal, however, in the edge region from which the particles are lost, so the zero plasma pressure (β) TF should be a reasonable approximation for our simulations. Test simulations were performed with one misaligned coil set each for SPARC and ARC, using a toroidally symmetric correction to Bφ meant to approximate the plasma contribution, and the results agreed within statistical uncertainty (see § 2.1). For the ARC simulations, coil sets were chosen with random misalignments in the radial and toroidal directions selected from Gaussian distributions with standard deviations σ ranging from 0.5 to 8 cm, rejecting misalignments greater than 1.5σ. These misalignments are expected to be significantly larger than the actual assembly tolerances of the ARC coils. Out of hundreds of randomly generated coil sets, one was chosen per misalignment type and σ which most closely matched the mean

2.1. Statistical uncertainty in loss calculations The statistical uncertainty arising from the use of a relatively small number of markers to represent a much larger number of physical particles is estimated in this work by the statistical method of bootstrapping. For each simulation of N markers performed for ARC, a new set of N markers, allowing for replacement, was sampled 10 000 times for the smaller simulations with misaligned coils and 1000 times for the larger simulations with either a 2-D field or perfectly aligned coils. From each new marker set, the percentage of alpha power loss was recalculated, and the error was taken to be the standard deviation of this sample. For calculating the error from ripple-induced losses (which, as previously described, are determined by subtracting the losses from an axisymmetric ARC from the losses found using each coil set), the error is taken to be only the error from the simulations including 3-D fields. The true error would be the root-squared sum of the bootstrapping error from both the axisymmetric and 3-D simulations, but as we are subtracting the same value (0.824 %) from each of the 3-D simulations, the error in this value will not contribute to the relative error between the different simulations, which is our primary concern in the following analysis.

On the other hand, the relationship between Eqa at ρ = 0.99 in the different ripple fields for ARC and their ripple-induced alpha power loss is nearly monotonic; any non-monotonic behaviour is within the statistical error calculated for the loss. 3.1. Additional misalignment types Previous work on SPARC considered not only radial and toroidal misalignments, but also vertical shifts (‘up/down misalignments’) and vertical tilts (rotation of the TF coils around ˆR). The latter were found to have negligible impact on (vacuum) TF ripple throughout the plasma, and therefore, these misalignments were not included when simulating alpha losses. Vertical shifts also had a negligible impact on vacuum ripple at the midplane, but well off the midplane (at Z = 0.5 and 0.75 m), the ripple induced was close to that from toroidal misalignments. Simulations of alpha loss were performed for SPARC with vertical coil shifts, and the alpha losses were found to be increased over the nominal case, but lower than the losses induced by toroidal and radial misalignments (Scott et al. 2020). Because toroidal and radial misalignments were expected, based on these results, to induce the highest losses, vertical shifts and tilts of the coils were not explored in the initial simulations performed for ARC. We attempt now to apply the metric of quasisymmetry error to fields created with these misalignment types in order to predict what alpha losses might be induced. What is the cause of the higher-than-expected ripple losses induced by vertical shifts and tilts of the coils in ARC? It is not explained by either TF ripple or QA error, as both metrics (including both vacuum TF ripple and the ripple of the full, finite-β field) are significantly lower across the entire plasma for these two new misalignment types compared with the previous two. Examining these misalignment types further, we find that there is a significant difference in the poloidal mode number of the perturbations they introduce in the magnetic field strength. Considering the case of each misalignment with the largest σ and looking at the ρ = 0.99 flux surface, we find that, for the toroidal misalignments, 96 % of the QA error comes from m = 0 modes, while for the radial misalignments, 40 % comes from these modes, and for the vertical shifts and tilts, only between 5 % and 7 % comes from m = 0 modes. We can also look for modes in the perturbed field which resonate with rational surfaces in the plasma. The minimum q in the field used in this paper (which, again, excludes the plasma contribution to Bφ, and thus differs from the 2-D equilibrium field reported in Hillesheim et al. 2026) is 0.86, and it reaches a value of around 3.23 near the edge. Considering only modes with 0.86 ⩽m/n ⩽3.23, we find they make up 1 % of the QA error for the radial misalignments, 0.2 % for the toroidal misalignments and 3 % for both the vertical shifts and tilts. Examining Poincaré plots of these magnetic fields, generated with ASCOT5, it can be seen that, in fact, all misalignment types but the toroidal case see significant stochasticity in the edge, usually beginning near or past the 3/2 flux surface. This may be a limit of the methods used in this work, as in reality, the plasma would heal some of this stochasticity, as well as the large islands produced by the misalignments. The choice to assume 2-D flux surfaces and treat the ripple as a small perturbation may not be valid for such large misalignments. An analysis which recalculates the equilibrium field in three dimensions before calculating the TF ripple and quasisymmetry error would likely produce more reliable results, but is beyond the scope of this work. We can, however, consider here an adjusted form of Eqa which only takes into account those modes in which m/n is within a certain range. 4. Application to SPARC Next, we will apply this method to misaligned coil sets for SPARC, which is in a more advanced stage of its design and thus has more information on alignment tolerances. Assuming the TF coils designed for SPARC move as rigid bodies, the following constraints are applied. First, coils are not allowed to move in the ˆZ (vertical) direction, as alignment is expected to be precise in this direction. Next, a line segment is defined in cylindrical coordinates (R, φ, Z) by the two points P1a = (R1, (nπ)/9, −Z1) and P1b = (R1, (nπ)/9, +Z1), where n ∈[0, 17] is the TF coil index, R1 is the innermost radial point of the TF coil case and Z1 = 1.21 m. To determine the position and tilt of the coil, P1a and P1b are allowed to move by up to ±2 mm in both ˆR and ˆφ as defined at the nominal coil position. During this process, the additional point P2 = (R2, (nπ)/9, 0), where R2 is the outermost radial position of the TF coil case, is held at constant φ, although it is allowed to shift radially and vertically as is necessary to maintain the rigid shape of the coil. Finally, after misaligning points P1a and P1b, P2 is allowed to move by ±1 mm by rotating the outer leg of the coil around the midpoint of the line segment between P1a and P1b. This process provides a somewhat conservative estimate of possible misalignments, as more recent work on SPARC assembly tolerances suggests that the inner leg will be more tightly constrained in the toroidal direction than in this work.

Several rippled magnetic fields were created and used in simulations for SPARC. Case C, an attempt at finding the worst case coil set (within the given tolerances), was constructed as follows: for coils n ∈[0, 8], P1a, P1b and P2 were shifted the maximum allowed extent in −ˆφ (as defined at the nominal coil position). A simulation was also performed for the final coil design at their predicted operating position (although not shrunk slightly, as will be the case in operation), with perfectly aligned coils, and the alpha power loss was found to be only 0.04 % lower (a 2 % variation in the power loss value) than that found with the case A field in this work. 5. Comparison with near-QA stellarator equilibria Finally, we ask, how do rippled tokamak equilibria compare with near-QA stellarator equilibria? Does it make sense to analyse rippled tokamaks using methods developed for QS stellarators? Figure 7 shows Eqa across the plasma for ARC and SPARC with perfectly aligned coils, as well as for several QA stellarator designs. The first is the free-boundary NCSX equilibrium, derived from the publicly available coil set designed for the partially constructed stellarator. The remaining four are variations on the Landreman–Paul QA designs (Landreman & Paul 2022), with (‘QA + Well-LP’) and without (‘QA-LP’) a Mercier stable magnetic well, as approximated by different sample coil sets in Wechsung et al. (2022). Assuming a major radius of 1 m and a set of 16 coils composed of 4 unique coil designs repeated 4 times, the coil sets were optimised while setting the upper limit Lmax on the combined length of the 4 unique coils to either 18 or 24 m. (In comparison, the average filament in the SPARC coil representation used here is 10.8 m; the ratio of average coil length to major radius for SPARC is thus 5.9, in between the values of 4.5 and 6 for the QA coil sets.) It can be seen that the QA error in ARC and SPARC is significantly lower (by factors of between 1/54x and 1/380x) than that of NCSX across the entire plasma; while cases B and C for SPARC are not plotted here, they also have more than an order of magnitude lower Eqa across the entire plasma than NCSX, showing that even with the worst misalignments within assembly tolerances, a rippled tokamak like SPARC is still significantly more QS than a moderately optimised QA stellarator like NCSX. However, depending on the coil length assumed, the Landreman–Paul QA designs may achieve more precise quasi-axisymmetry than ARC and SPARC across the outer half of the plasma volume. This is not to say that we can thus assume that highly optimised QS stellarators will outperform tokamaks in fast ion confinement. As previously stated, quasisymmetry error cannot necessarily be used to predict fast ion losses across different device types, as there are additional factors which determine confinement, such as magnetic shear, device size and plasma density and temperature. As-built stellarators, which must also consider engineering feasibility and other qualities, such as neutron shielding in power plants, may not be able to achieve such precise quasisymmetry. In addition, as coils can never be perfectly constructed or assembled, the question remains whether misalignments and other deviations from design in stellarator coils will be more or less deleterious for particle confinement than in tokamaks. Tokamaks also have the advantage of being able to run a variety of plasma equilibria, all of which will likely have similar levels of quasisymmetry if using the same coil set, while highly optimised stellarators are typically designed to achieve strong quasisymmetry with one specific set of coil currents and plasma pressure. Regardless, it has been shown that tokamaks constructed from discrete coil sets lie between moderately and highly optimised QA stellarators when it comes to deviations from perfect quasisymmetry across much of the plasma – particularly the edge, from which fast ions tend to be lost – and that metrics used in stellarators to quantify quasisymmetry and optimise fast ion confinement can also be used to characterise alpha losses from tokamaks with realistic coil misalignments. Considering this, physically constructed, as opposed to idealised, tokamaks can be considered to be a special case of near-QA device, and there may be additional techniques from stellarator theory which can be applied to their design and simulation.

6. Conclusions In this work, it was found that 3-D ripple fields created by the discrete TF coils and possible assembly errors in SPARC and ARC can be analysed with the metric of quasisymmetry error, often used as a proxy for fast ion losses in stellarators, and that this metric strongly correlates with loss of alpha power in these two tokamaks, other than in the case of large vertical shifts or tilts of the TF coils. In this latter case, an adjusted form of Eqa which includes only those modes in the field strength which resonate with the safety factor near the edge serves as a better proxy for loss. However, the misalignments considered for ARC in this paper are far outside expected tolerances. For the fields considered for SPARC, in which misalignments were limited based on assembly tolerances, the traditional form of Eqa predicted alpha power loss with a correlation coefficient of 0.97. This shows that, for relevant cases, the simple form of Eqa should serve as a strong proxy for losses in rippled tokamaks, while the adjusted version mostly serves as a diagnostic for determining which fields will become stochastic in the edge and therefore require a more rigorous treatment. It was also shown that even with perfectly aligned TF coils, SPARC and ARC have similar or higher values of QA error to highly optimised QA stellarators with simple coil designs, justifying the decision to treat these rippled tokamak equilibria as a special case of near-QA devices. The work shown in this paper did not consider the impact of RMPs, although both SPARC and ARC will contain coils capable of inducing RMPs if needed for ELM suppression (Sweeney et al. 2020; Leuthold et al. 2026). If the 3-D fields induced by these coils are found to break QA severely enough in the plasma edge for the field in this region to become stochastic, then another metric may be more appropriate for the analysis of equilibria with applied RMPs. In addition, if the use of RMPs is found to be necessary in future devices like ARC, and the QA error induced by these perturbations is large compared with error fields from TF coil misalignments, it may be possible to relax tolerances on TF coil alignment without significantly worsening alpha losses – although this does not consider other negative impacts of misaligned TF coils. There may also be additional metrics which, while more complicated to compute than QA error, better characterise losses. For instance, there are the metrics ΓC and Γα, sometimes used in stellarator optimisation, which attempt to more directly quantify the omnigeneity of a given field (Nemov et al. 2008; Velasco et al. 2021). In addition, it has been shown that a significant driver of losses is the resonance between field asymmetries and the ‘orbit pitch’ of the fast ion orbits (rather than the field line pitch, which is considered in the modified Eqa used in this paper), which breaks conservation of the second adiabatic invariant and, in the case of multiple overlapping resonances, can drive the fast ion orbits to become stochastic. This effect is especially relevant to RMPs in tokamaks, which have been shown to drive losses of fast ions in KSTAR and EAST due to resonant interactions with the ion orbits (Shinohara et al. 2018; He et al. 2025). It has been discussed in Chambliss, Paul & Hudson (2025) that even small deviations from quasisymmetry in stellarators can lead to increased losses when these errors are resonant with fast ion drift orbits, and simulated alpha losses from the Helios stellarator design have been characterised based on this resonance (von der Linden et al. 2026). A further modified version of Eqa which considers deviations from QA resonant with the alpha drift orbits, rather than with the safety factor near the edge, may better explain alpha losses, as might

a metric which quantifies the width or overlap of alpha drift islands, as explored in Shinohara et al. (2018). However, this more complicated analysis, which requires the energy and pitch of the alphas to be taken into account, is left for future work. While QA error is insufficient for predicting losses between significantly different devices, or in cases where coil misalignments are very large and fields become stochastic, it correlates well with losses across variations on a specific device when misalignments are not too large. The calculation of QA error requires only the calculation of the ripple field on a 3-D grid and a simple analysis, which is much less computationally expensive than Monte Carlo orbit-following simulations to determine alpha losses – once the 3-D field is calculated, finding the QA error takes only a few minutes on a single CPU, while the ASCOT5 simulations required around 10 CPU node hours on Perlmutter for the smallest simulations performed for ARC in this paper and 80 for the largest. This suggests that, as in stellarator optimisation, QA error may be used as a proxy for ripple-induced alpha loss in tokamaks for rapid design iterations of TF coils and evaluation of the impact of different potential assembly errors – one which is faster and simpler than full orbitfollowing simulations and more accurate than the traditional tokamak metric of TF ripple.
